extracted.intended_audience: regulatory agencies, lawmakers, advocacy groups, technology vendors, and law enforcement
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and policy recommendations to detect, deter, and remediate fraudulent or deceptive submissions to government public-comment processes (rulemakings, congressional messages, petitions) and best practices for intermediaries and agencies handling mass submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandate Disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Intermediaries must disclose, with each comment or message submitted, the intermediary’s identity and the identities of any parties that assisted in generating or submitting the comments and messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure can be within the comment text (e.g., “This comment was solicited and submitted by Company A, on behalf of Non-Profit X.”) or separately in viewable metadata attached to the comment (e.g., registration for mass submissions). The disclosure should be made public as part of the comment process to inform public debate and help identify abuses. Agencies should require advocacy groups that sponsor or run campaigns, not just their vendors, be identified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold intermediaries to account
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocacy groups and vendors that submit comments or messages should be held responsible for fake submissions they generate or submit to government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should impose consequences that vary based on factors such as the number of fake submissions attributable to the intermediary, whether submissions were inadvertent or intentional, and what preventive measures the intermediary had adopted. Consequences may include civil fines and suspension of submission privileges. Enforcement should place responsibility on parties best positioned to detect and prevent fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit deceptive and unauthorized comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawmakers should outlaw knowingly submitting, or causing to be submitted, multiple comments or messages intended to deceive or submitted on behalf of someone else without taking reasonable measures to verify express, informed consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A federal or state statute should (i) prohibit these behaviors, (ii) require reasonable verification of express informed consent before submitting on someone’s behalf, (iii) include meaningful penalties (substantial civil fines) to make fraud costly, and (iv) expressly authorize state attorneys general to enforce the statute when residents’ information is misused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthen impersonation laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Update criminal impersonation statutes to address mass impersonation in electronic comments and messages to government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amend laws to provide substantial penalties when many individuals are impersonated before a government agency or official, recognizing existing misdemeanor statutes were not designed to deter large-scale misuse of hundreds of thousands of identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement technical safeguards against automated submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should deploy technical measures to detect and block submissions generated by automated software or bots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate first steps include CAPTCHAs to block automated submissions, but agencies should also implement a suite of measures (rate limiting, traffic analysis, third-party bot-detection services, anomaly detection) appropriate to their systems. Agencies with budget shortfalls should consider partnerships with private-sector actors to implement technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require identity verification and registration for mass/API submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Entities seeking to submit comments in bulk via APIs or other mass-submission channels must first identify and validate their identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use identity-validation services (as GSA does for Regulations.gov) to verify entities authorized to use APIs. Require that advocacy groups sponsoring campaigns be identified, not just vendors, and ensure identifying information is made available to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require express, informed consent before submitting on someone’s behalf
rubrics_metrics.description: Intermediaries must obtain and document express, informed consent from individuals before submitting a comment or message to the government on their behalf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlements cited require robust disclosures to consumers and prohibit submission to government unless consumers have provided express informed consent. Consent practices should be clear, documented, and verifiable; submissions based on co-registration or other incentives must not be treated as consent absent explicit authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor and vet vendors and subcontractors; retain records
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocacy groups and other campaign organizers must conduct careful monitoring of subcontractors and retain records that facilitate oversight and investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracts and campaigns should require vendor oversight, auditing rights, and retention of records about consent and the mechanics of lead collection. Settlements require monitoring of subcontractors and record retention to enable investigations into potential misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose campaign sponsorship, funding, and role in solicitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaign organizers and sponsors should be identified publicly so the source and funding behind comment drives are transparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid obscuring funding by routing campaigns through unrelated advocacy groups or non-profits. Disclose sponsors and funders in campaign solicitations and in docket metadata so the public and press can identify interested parties and potential conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impose meaningful civil fines and penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil penalties for fraudulent or deceptive mass-comment activity should be substantial enough to deter misconduct, not merely a cost of doing business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutes and agency rules should define penalty structures scaled to harm and volume; state attorneys general should be expressly authorized to seek enforcement and penalties where residents’ data are misused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve anonymous comment options while protecting against fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Reforms should not foreclose anonymous comments, which can protect privacy, but should include safeguards so anonymous participation is not exploited for mass deception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design verification, disclosure, and anti-fraud protections that preserve legitimate anonymity (e.g., a comment signed “anonymous” should not be penalized for an intent to deceive) while preventing automated, bulk, or impersonating submissions from undermining the docket.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies should mandate adoption of reforms and provide resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal agencies and legislatures should have authority to adopt the recommended reforms uniformly and should provide resources to implement them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandating disclosure, technical safeguards, and accountability rules at the agency level — and funding their implementation — will ensure uniform application and make investigations and enforcement feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pay-for-volume procurement and prioritize quality; watch for red flags
rubrics_metrics.description: Clients (advocacy groups and industry sponsors) should not reward vendors solely for volume of leads/comments; procurement should emphasize quality, verifiable consent, and controls against fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Red flags include vendors refusing to show live traffic, providing staged 'show-me' sites, or supplying record sets that cannot be validated. Contracts should require proof of consent, real-time monitoring, and immediate remediation on detection of fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require metadata and public traceability for submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass submissions should include machine-readable metadata or docket fields that trace submission provenance (which intermediary, sponsor, and vendor produced the record).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making structured provenance data available publicly facilitates journalistic and regulatory review and helps law enforcement trace fraudulent comment origins. Agencies should add document-level or record-level fields to store vendor/sponsor provenance.
